'''''Daphne gnidium''''', the '''flax-leaved daphne''', is a poisonous [[evergreen]] shrub from the northern and western Mediterranean region, with narrow, dense dark-green [[foliage]] and white fragrant flowers.

==Description==
''Daphne gnidium'' is a shrub with upright branches that grow to {{convert|1.5|to|2|m|abbr=on}} tall. The dense [[lanceolate]] leaves are dark green with sticky undersides. It bears fragrant white flowers in late [[Spring (season)|spring]] or early [[summer]]. The fruit is a [[drupe]], and is round and red, about {{convert|8|mm|abbr=on}} diameter. They are produced during [[autumn]].<ref name="W11">{{cite web|url=http://www.shootgardening.co.uk/plant/daphne-gnidium |title=Daphne gnidium (Flax-leaved daphne) |author= |date= |website=shootgardening.co.uk |accessdate=22 January 2011 }}</ref><ref name="aW1">{{cite web|url=http://www.botanical-online.com/fotosdahpne.htm|title='Daphne gnidium L. (''Daphne'')|author=|date=|website=botanical-online.com|accessdate=22 January 2011}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
Three [[subspecies]] are currently accepted by the [[Plants of the World Online]] database:<ref name="POWO"/>
*''Daphne gnidium'' subsp. ''gnidium'' – Europe, coastal northwest Africa, Canary Islands<ref name="Ramos"/>
*''Daphne gnidium'' subsp. ''maritima'' <small>(Rozeira) Capelo, J.C.Costa, Esp.Santo & Lousã</small> – western Portugal<ref name="Ramos"/>
*''Daphne gnidium'' subsp. ''mauritanica'' <small>(Nieto Fel.) Halda</small> – northwest Africa in the Atlas Mountains<ref name="Ramos"/>
Recent genetic analysis however suggests that the Atlas Mountains populations are strongly distinct, and would be better treated as a separate species ''Daphne mauritanica'' <small>Nieto Fel.</small>, but conversely, that the western Portuguese population is not distinct from the rest of the European populations, so subsp. ''maritima'' should be regarded as a [[synonym (taxonomy)|synonym]] of subsp. ''gnidium''.<ref name="Ramos">{{cite journal | last1=Ramos‐Capón | first1=Cristina | last2=Vargas | first2=Pablo | last3=Pomeda‐Gutiérrez | first3=Fernando | last4=Martín‐Hernanz | first4=Sara | title=Time‐calibrated phylogeny of Daphne (Thymelaeaceae): Pre‐mediterranean temporal origin of the sclerophyllous Daphne gnidium | journal=Journal of Systematics and Evolution | volume=62 | issue=1 | date=2024 | issn=1674-4918 | doi=10.1111/jse.13018 | doi-access=free | pages=20–37 | url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdfdirect/10.1111/jse.13018 | access-date=2025-08-21| hdl=10261/370412 | hdl-access=free }}</ref>

==Habitat==
''Daphne gnidium'' grows well in sandy loam. It grows in fields, woodlands, [[garrigue]]s, and hillsides, and is native to the areas surrounding the north and west of the [[Mediterranean Sea]] in southern Europe from [[Portugal]] east to [[Greece]], and northwestern Africa in [[Morocco]], [[Algeria]], and [[Tunisia]].<ref name="POWO"/>

==Toxicity==
''Daphne gnidium'' contains the [[toxin]]s [[mezerein]] and [[daphnetoxin]]. All parts of the plant are considered highly poisonous. Skin contact with the [[sap]] can cause [[dermatitis]]<ref name="W21">{{cite web|url=http://www.botanical-online.com/alcaloidesdaphneangles.htm|title=''Daphne gnidium'' L|author=|date=|website=botanical-online.com/|accessdate=22 January 2011}}</ref> The chance of death is small yet possible within 6 hours after direct consumption. At least severe anabolic and indigestive reactions are expected, which may also trigger lethal allergic reactions.{{citation needed|date=November 2017}}
